questions.scenario: Vireo Labs has just acquired a nine-year-old Rails monolith plus four satellite services. A new platform engineer asks whether anyone should run `/init` in the monolith before the team starts migrating it to a service-based architecture.
questions.stem: What should the platform team decide before anyone generates a CLAUDE.md for that repository?

options.text: Decide what the file is for. `/init` produces standing instructions that load into every session in the repo, so it should hold only stable facts and conventions — build commands, layout, the rules that are always true. Anything that reads like a procedure belongs in a skill that loads on demand, and a repository with nothing stable and non-obvious to record is legitimately better off with no CLAUDE.md at all.
Run `/init` in every repository the team touches, including throwaway spikes, so no engineer ever has to rediscover a build command.
Hand-write the file first and never run `/init`, because generated instructions are generic and will drift away from how the team actually works.
Run `/init` at the repository root and then split the result into a CLAUDE.md in every top-level directory, so each area's guidance loads as soon as a session starts there.

questions.explanation: The decision is about what the artefact is for, not about generating one per repo. A CLAUDE.md is standing context: it is paid for in every session in that repository, so its value is density of stable, non-obvious fact. The skills page draws exactly this line — create a skill when you keep pasting the same instructions or when a section of CLAUDE.md has grown into a procedure rather than a fact. A repo you are about to delete has no business carrying configuration, and one with nothing stable to record does not need a file. Hand-writing first is a reasonable preference but not the governing constraint, and per-directory CLAUDE.md files are not how directory-scoped guidance is meant to work — that is what path-scoped `.claude/rules/` with `paths:` globs are for, and they load when a matching file is read.

whyWrong.B: Configuration in a throwaway repo costs nothing and pays nothing back, and it becomes maintenance debt the moment someone copies it. The rule of thumb is density of stable content, not one file per directory on disk.
whyWrong.C: Writing by hand is a style preference, not a correctness condition; `/init` output is a starting draft that the docs explicitly expect you to review and trim. Refusing to use it does not make the placement question go away.
whyWrong.D: A CLAUDE.md per top-level directory is a recurring cost paid whenever a session starts there, and it does not achieve directory-scoped loading — a subdirectory's file loads for sessions that start there, not for a root session that later touches one file. Path-scoped rules are the mechanism for that.

questions.mindset: CLAUDE.md is standing context paid for every session: facts that are always true go there, procedures go in skills, and no file is a valid answer.

questions.scenario: Meridian Payments runs a shared `.claude/settings.json` in the ledger repository that allows `Bash(git log *)` and `Bash(pnpm test *)`. An engineer's `~/.claude/settings.json` allows `Bash(docker *)`, and their `settings.local.json` allows `Read(./secrets/**)`. A colleague claims the local file must have replaced the committed one.
questions.stem: Which statement about how Claude Code resolves these three settings files is correct?

options.text: The highest-precedence file wins for every key, so the user's `~/.claude/settings.json` replaces the committed file entirely and none of the ledger's allow rules apply.

It depends on the key. Scalar keys such as `model` or `permissions.defaultMode` resolve to the highest level that sets them — managed settings, then the command line, then project local, then shared project, then user. List keys such as `permissions.allow` are merged across the files instead, so all three allow lists apply.
Settings files do not stack at all. Claude Code reads project local, then shared project, then user, and the first file that contains the key in question supplies every value in it.
User settings outrank everything except managed settings, because they sit closest to the process, so the colleague is right that the committed allow rules are shadowed.

questions.explanation: Precedence is per key, and it splits on shape. The documented stack, highest first, is managed settings, command line, project local (`.claude/settings.local.json`), shared project (`.claude/settings.json`), user (`~/.claude/settings.json`). For a scalar key, the highest level that sets it supplies the value — which is why a project `model` beats a user `model` even though user is normally thought of as more personal. List keys are the exception: when the same list key such as `permissions.allow` appears in more than one file, Claude Code combines the lists rather than picking one, so each file can add entries without removing another file's. A few keys have their own rule — `fallbackModel` is an ordered chain where position carries meaning and is therefore taken whole from the highest-precedence file that defines it.

whyWrong.A: That describes a whole-file override, which is not how the stack works. List keys merge, and each scalar key is resolved on its own, so the committed allow rules survive alongside the user's.
whyWrong.C: This is the ordering right but the resolution rule wrong. Precedence is not first-file-wins: a lower level still supplies any key a higher level does not set, and lists accumulate.
whyWrong.D: User settings sit at the bottom of the stack, not the top. Project local outranks shared project, which outranks user — the ordering people assume from how configuration usually works is reversed here.

questions.mindset: Precedence resolves per key, and lists merge: check the key's shape before assuming one file replaces another.

questions.scenario: Meridian's platform team commits `"permissions": {"defaultMode": "auto"}` in the ledger repository's `.claude/settings.json`, expecting every engineer who clones it to land in auto mode by default. Nobody's session does.
questions.stem: What is happening, and what is the correct fix?

options.text: The key is valid but sits below a user-level `defaultMode` the engineers already have. Remove the key from the user settings files and the committed value will apply.
`permissions.defaultMode` is ignored in any settings file. Auto mode can only be selected with Shift+Tab or `--permission-mode auto`, so the team should document that instead of committing the key.
The values `auto` and `bypassPermissions` specifically do not take effect from project or local settings. Put the key in user or managed settings, or pass `--permission-mode` for one session.
The key only applies once each teammate trusts the folder, and the trust step is what is failing. The fix is to add the repository to the trusted list on each machine.

questions.explanation: Some keys are scope-restricted by design, and `permissions.defaultMode` is one of them: the values `auto` and `bypassPermissions` do not take effect from project or local settings, so committing them in `.claude/settings.json` is a no-op for everyone who clones the repo. Set the key in user or managed settings instead, or pass `--permission-mode` when you want one specific session to start that way. Note that `default` is unaffected — only those two values are restricted. Trust is a separate mechanism that gates `permissions.allow` rules, `permissions.additionalDirectories`, `extraKnownMarketplaces` and most `env` values until a teammate accepts the workspace; `deny` and `ask` rules apply immediately, which is why a security rule in a committed file works before trust and an allow rule does not.

whyWrong.A: There is no user-level value in play, and removing one would not help even if there were — the restriction is that this key's risky values are ignored at the project and local levels at all, regardless of what sits above them.
whyWrong.B: Overstating the restriction. `default` does take effect from project and local settings; only the `auto` and `bypassPermissions` values are refused there, precisely so a repository cannot quietly opt a whole team into reduced scrutiny.
whyWrong.D: Trust gating is real but it is the wrong gate here: `defaultMode` is not a trust-gated key. Even a fully trusted clone would still ignore these two values from a committed project file.

questions.mindset: A key a repository can set but cannot escalate: check each key's documented Scope, because a committed value may be ignored on purpose.

questions.scenario: Meridian commits a `.claude/settings.json` with `theme`, `modelPicker`, `permissions.allow` and an `env` block carrying `DATABASE_URL`. On a teammate's fresh clone the theme and the picker do not take effect and the database variable is empty, while the allow rules work once they trust the folder.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements explain that pattern accurately? Choose TWO.

options.text: `theme` and `modelPicker` never apply from a repository file at all. Look in the settings index's Scope column: keys marked `User, local, or managed` — or `Managed`, or `Global config` — cannot be delivered by the shared project file, so they belong in user or managed settings.

`modelPicker` is the exception that proves the rule: it is ignored in project and local settings but does merge with user settings, so a teammate with their own picker still picks up the committed rows.

Most `env` values from a shared project file wait for workspace trust, which is why the variable only populates after the teammate accepts the folder. `deny` and `ask` permission rules are the exceptions that apply right away.
All four keys are valid from a repository file and the only variable is trust, which every key waits on equally — so accepting the folder once should make the theme and picker appear.

questions.explanation: Two different mechanisms are at work and they are easy to conflate. The first is scope: some keys are simply not deliverable by the shared project file. The settings reference carries a Scope column, and entries marked `User, local, or managed`, `Managed` or `Global config` never apply from `.claude/settings.json`, which is how the reference tells you where the key has to live. `modelPicker` is the sharpest case — it holds one ordered list plus a replace flag, so Claude Code never merges rows from two sources, and it ignores the key in project and local settings. The second mechanism is trust: `permissions.allow` rules, `permissions.additionalDirectories`, `extraKnownMarketplaces` and most `env` values apply only after each teammate trusts the folder, while `deny` and `ask` rules take effect immediately. That is why a committed deny rule is the safer thing to ship and a committed allow rule is not a guarantee until trust lands.

whyWrong.B: `modelPicker` is the strongest illustration of the rule, not an exception to it. Because position and the replace flag carry meaning, rows can never be merged, so the key is ignored in project and local settings outright.
whyWrong.D: Trust is uniform and separate; it is not the explanation for the theme or the picker. Those keys are scope-restricted, so a trusted clone still will not pick them up from the repository file.

questions.mindset: Two separate gates: a key's documented Scope decides whether a repo can set it at all, and workspace trust decides whether it applies yet.

questions.scenario: Meridian's ledger repository commits a `permissions.deny` list covering `Read(./.env)` and `Bash(terraform apply *)`, plus an `allow` list covering `Bash(git diff *)`. On a brand-new clone a teammate confirms that reads of `.env` are refused immediately, but `git diff` still prompts and the allow list appears to be doing nothing.
questions.stem: What is the correct reading of the two lists' behaviour on that clone?

options.text: Neither list has loaded yet. Both `allow` and `deny` rules from a committed file wait for workspace trust, so the deny behaviour the engineer observed must be coming from a managed settings file on their machine.
Both lists loaded and both are working, but `allow` rules grant nothing until a rule is matched after trust, so the prompt on `git diff` is expected and unrelated to trust.

This is the documented asymmetry. `deny` and `ask` rules from the committed file apply right away, while `allow` rules, `permissions.additionalDirectories`, `extraKnownMarketplaces` and most `env` values wait until the teammate trusts the folder.
The deny list is being honoured only because `Read(./.env)` is a path rule rather than a bare tool name. Bare-tool deny rules from a repository file wait for trust exactly like allow rules do.

questions.explanation: Restrictive rules are meant to be effective the moment they are present, and permissive ones are not — that is the whole point of the asymmetry. On a fresh clone, `permissions.deny` and `permissions.ask` rules committed in `.claude/settings.json` apply immediately, so a repository can protect something before anyone has agreed to run anything. By contrast `permissions.allow` rules, `permissions.additionalDirectories`, `extraKnownMarketplaces` and most `env` values take effect only after each teammate trusts the folder, because a repository that could pre-approve a command by being cloned would be a privilege-escalation path. The practical consequence for a team is that deny and ask are the enforceable half of a committed permission policy, and allow rules are a convenience that arrives after trust.

whyWrong.A: This has the trust gate applied uniformly and therefore contradicts the observed behaviour. Deny rules are the documented exception that applies immediately, so no managed file is needed to explain the `.env` refusal.
whyWrong.B: Trust is the actual gate for the allow list, so calling the prompt 'unrelated to trust' contradicts the mechanism. The fix is to have the teammate trust the folder, not to re-examine the rule.
whyWrong.D: Path rules are ordinary permission rules and are not gated differently from bare tool names. The distinction is allow versus deny and ask, not path rules versus bare names.

questions.mindset: Committed deny and ask rules apply on sight; committed allow rules are a convenience that only lands once the folder is trusted.

questions.scenario: Meridian adds a long permission list to the shared `.claude/settings.json`. On one engineer's machine a single entry is dropped with a warning about a malformed permission rule and everything else works. On the CI runner the same file is ignored completely with no visible message, and a `pnpm lint` rule never actually takes effect.
questions.stem: What is the difference between these two symptoms, and what is the correct diagnostic step?

options.text: They are the same failure. The warning is just a courtesy that only the interactive build emits, so the CI runner is doing the same thing quietly.

The local case is a Settings Warning: only individual entries fail, Claude Code skips those values and keeps the rest of the file. The CI case is worse and less visible — a `-p` run shows no dialog, so run `claude doctor` to see exactly what was rejected.

The local case is a Settings Error, which invalidates the whole file, while the CI case is a warning about a single entry. The diagnostic is to open the file in an editor with the published JSON schema attached.
Neither is a Claude Code behaviour. A file with any invalid entry is rejected atomically by git, so the working copy the CI runner checked out simply cannot contain a mixed-validity file.

questions.explanation: Claude Code distinguishes partial from total breakage, and the interactive/non-interactive split is what makes the CI case dangerous. A Settings Error is invalid JSON or a value the schema rejects in a user, project or local file: at the start of an interactive session you get a dialog offering to fix it with Claude's help, exit, or continue without the broken settings. A Settings Warning is narrower — only individual entries fail, such as a malformed permission rule or an unknown hook event name, and Claude Code skips those values and keeps the rest of the file in effect. A `-p` run shows no dialog at all; unless a managed settings document itself cannot be parsed, it skips the broken file or values and continues with the rest. So the CI symptom is real and silent, and the documented diagnostic in both cases is `claude doctor` for the detail behind `/status`.

whyWrong.A: Collapsing the two cases loses the part that actually matters operationally. The interactive warning and the silent CI skip are different severities of the same class, and the silent one is why a rule can be absent in production for months.
whyWrong.C: The severities are inverted, and the schema URL only helps with syntax and value validation in an editor. It cannot tell you which entries a headless run dropped.
whyWrong.D: Git has no opinion on JSON validity; it commits whatever is on disk. Claude Code's own partial-and-total distinction is what produces the two different behaviours.

questions.mindset: A headless run has no dialog, so a broken settings file degrades silently — after any unexplained `-p` behaviour, read the diagnostics, not the file.

questions.scenario: Meridian's monorepo is checked out at `/repo`, and an engineer habitually starts Claude Code from `/repo/packages/frontend`. She has approved a standing `Bash(pnpm test *)` grant several times. A colleague at the repo root cannot find any of those grants, and a worktree session appears to have lost them entirely.
questions.stem: Where does Claude Code actually place and read `.claude/settings.local.json` in these three cases?

options.text: In the directory you started in, in all three cases. Each starting directory keeps its own local file, which is why the root-based colleague sees nothing and why a worktree behaves independently.
Beside `.claude/settings.json` in whatever directory Claude Code was started, so a worktree uses the worktree's own pair and the root colleague sees only root-level grants.

At the repository root in all three cases: if you start in a subdirectory of a git repository, Claude Code reads and writes that file at the root and applies the approval across the whole repository. In a worktree it uses the file at the main checkout's root. A couple of documented exceptions qualify the root location — outside a git repository, when the repo root is your home directory, and when the root or its `.git`/`.claude` entry is not owned by you — where the file stays alongside `settings.json`.
In `~/.claude/` keyed by project path, so the grants are global per repository and follow you into worktrees automatically, which is why the worktree session kept them.

questions.explanation: Personal-per-project grants are repository-scoped, not directory-scoped, and that is deliberate: a permission you grant while working in one package is a permission you granted in that repository. If you start Claude Code in a subdirectory of a git repository, it reads and writes `.claude/settings.local.json` at the repository root and applies the approval across the whole repository, which is exactly why the root-based colleague sees the grants. In a worktree, it uses the file at the main checkout's root. The exceptions are documented rather than accidental: outside a git repository, when the repository root is your home directory, on Windows, or when the repository root or its `.git` or `.claude` entry is not owned by your user, the local file stays with `settings.json`. One more detail worth knowing: in the path, a rule starting with `/` or a relative sandbox path anchors at the session's primary working directory rather than the repository root.

whyWrong.A: Per-starting-directory placement would make the root-based colleague's behaviour correct, but it is not how the file is stored — which is precisely the confusion this question is about.
whyWrong.B: Correct only in the exception cases. The normal rule is repository root, not the starting directory, and a worktree follows the main checkout rather than its own root.
whyWrong.D: The file is per project inside the project's `.claude/` directory, not in the user config directory. Storing it under `~/.claude/` would make it apply to every project on the machine, which is the user-scope behaviour this file explicitly avoids.

questions.mindset: Personal grants are repository-scoped, not directory-scoped: a grant made in one package is a grant in that repo, and a worktree follows the main checkout.

questions.scenario: Meridian's security team commits `permissions.deny` rules for `.env` and production deploy commands. The team also wanted to pre-approve `Bash(pnpm test *)` from the shared file, but the security review blocked it because it grants a capability before anyone has agreed to run the repository's code.
questions.stem: Which explanation of that asymmetry matches the documented behaviour?

options.text: There is no asymmetry. The security team's objection is sound but incidental: Claude Code applies both allow and deny rules from a repository file only after trust, so nothing from the file reaches a fresh clone.

The documented behaviour is narrower and slightly different: the local file's allow rules skip the workspace trust step, but only while the file is untracked. If it is tracked by git, the trust step applies to it too — which is exactly the state a freshly committed personal file is in.

Because the file is yours rather than the repository's, Claude Code applies its allow rules without the trust step — so committing the personal file would have been the fix and the security team was wrong to block it.
Trust only gates `permissions.deny`. Allow rules from a repository file have always applied immediately, so the pre-approval would have worked on the first clone.

questions.explanation: The nuance is that an untracked local file is treated as yours rather than as the repository's, so its allow rules apply without the workspace trust step. Track it in git and it becomes part of the repository, and the trust step applies to it as well. That is exactly the state a personal file lands in the moment someone commits it, and it is why the correct pattern is to keep `settings.local.json` untracked — Claude Code adds `**/.claude/settings.local.json` to your global git excludes the first time it writes the file, but if you create the file by hand and Claude Code has not written to it yet, you have to add the ignore yourself. Meanwhile the committed `deny` rules were never in doubt: deny and ask apply right away, which is what makes them the enforceable half of a shared policy.

whyWrong.A: It applies trust uniformly, which contradicts the observed immediate effect of the deny rules on a fresh clone and erases the untracked-versus-tracked distinction that is the actual rule.
whyWrong.C: It has the direction of the rule backwards and then draws the wrong conclusion. The local file skipping trust is precisely why it must stay out of version control; committing it puts it under trust like any other repository file.
whyWrong.D: Trust gates allow rules, not deny rules. Pre-approving a command from a file that arrives by cloning would be a capability grant nobody agreed to, so the security team's objection matches the design.

questions.mindset: An untracked local file is yours and skips trust; the moment you commit it, it is the repository's and trust applies — keep it untracked.

questions.scenario: Meridian's platform team edits the shared `.claude/settings.json` during an incident to add an `apiKeyHelper` and tighten a `deny` rule, without asking anyone to restart their sessions. Afterwards they notice the change landed in the running sessions, but an administrator's MDM-delivered policy change appears not to have.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about settings changes and running sessions are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Claude Code watches your settings files and reloads them when they change, applying most edits to a running session without a restart — including edits to `permissions`, `hooks`, and credential helpers such as `apiKeyHelper`. It runs the `ConfigChange` hook for each settings-file change it detects.

Some keys are read only once at session start, so an edit to one of them never reaches the running session. Admin-side keys such as `requiredMinimumVersion` are the documented examples, and managed settings arriving from MDM or the claude.ai console reach a running session on a schedule rather than on save.

Reload is universal, so a managed change from the console lands immediately everywhere. The only key that needs `/model` instead of a file edit is `model`, and only because of the prompt-cache cost of switching.
Because settings hot-reload, a change to `.claude/settings.local.json` is picked up immediately with no trust step involved. Trust is evaluated once per session at startup and never revisited.

questions.explanation: Hot reload is real and covers the edits teams make most often, which is why tightening a permission during an incident works on sessions that are already running. Claude Code watches the user, project, local and managed settings files and reloads on change, applying most edits without a restart, and it fires the `ConfigChange` hook for each settings-file change it detects. The exceptions matter just as much. A subset of keys is read once at session start, and admin-side keys such as `requiredMinimumVersion` are on that list, so an edit never reaches a live session. Managed sources also arrive on their own schedule — MDM and the claude.ai console do not push on save — which is why a policy change needs a session restart before `/status` will show the new source. And a few common keys have a documented mid-session route instead of a file edit: `model` via `/model`, `effortLevel` and `modelSettings` via `/effort`.

whyWrong.C: It overstates reload to cover managed delivery, which is exactly the case that does not land on save. It also misstates why `model` needs `/model`: each model has its own prompt cache, so the first request after a switch re-reads the conversation uncached — that is a cost note attached to the switch, not the reason a file edit is insufficient.
whyWrong.D: It confuses reload with trust. Trust is a workspace decision, and allow rules from a committed file still wait on it; reload only governs whether a change to an already-loaded source takes effect.

questions.mindset: Most settings edits hot-reload and fire `ConfigChange`; start-once keys and MDM-delivered policy need a restart, and managed sources never arrive on save.

questions.scenario: Meridian wants to try a new model on one engineer's machine for an afternoon without touching any settings file, and without disturbing what the team has committed.
questions.stem: Which invocation achieves that, and what are its documented boundaries?

options.text: `claude --settings '{"model": "claude-opus-5-5"}'`. It takes a path to a settings file or an inline JSON string, applies above the user, project and local files and below managed settings, lasts one session, and writes nothing. Keys you omit keep their file-based values, and it can set anything a user settings file can set but not `Managed` or `Global config` keys.

`claude --model claude-opus-5-5`. It is the documented one-session override for exactly this case, and because command-line arguments sit above project local, shared project and user settings, it also overrides managed settings.
Edit `~/.claude/settings.json`, start a session, then `git checkout` the file afterwards. The file is untracked by definition, so no commit is created and the change is invisible to the team.
`ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-opus-5-5 claude` in a subshell. Environment variables are the top level of the settings precedence stack, so nothing in any settings file can override them.

questions.explanation: `--settings` is the documented way to change a setting for one session without saving it. It accepts a path to a settings JSON file or an inline JSON string, and it merges what you pass with your settings files by the same rules as the other levels: a key you set here wins over the same key in local, project or user settings, and a key you omit keeps its file-based value. It sits at command-line level — above all four file levels and below managed settings — and it writes nothing, so the next session is back to normal. Its limits are explicit: it can set any key your user settings file can set, and it cannot set `Managed` or `Global config` keys. The flags for particular keys work the same way, since `--model` overrides the `model` setting and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` while `--effort` overrides `effortLevel` and `modelSettings` for the session.

whyWrong.B: `--model` is a legitimate one-session override, but the precedence claim is wrong and the limitation is fatal for this task. Managed settings are the top level, and a flag such as `--model` picks only from the models the organization allows — it cannot override a managed key.
whyWrong.C: Editing and reverting by hand works but is the wrong instrument: it risks leaving the change behind, it pollutes the working tree, and it cannot express a per-invocation experiment in a script. `--settings` exists precisely so this needs no edit at all.
whyWrong.D: Environment variables are explicitly not a level in the settings stack. Which of a variable or a settings key applies is decided per pair, not by precedence level, and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` exported in your shell applies over the `model` key from any file — but not over managed settings.

questions.mindset: To try a value without keeping it, pass it for the session — `--settings` for any key, or the key's own flag — and remember nothing writes back.

questions.scenario: Meridian's CI review job lets Claude run its normal tools, but a security reviewer asks that the job be unable to shell out at all — no Bash, no command execution, nothing that runs code on the runner — while still letting it read and edit files under the checkout.
questions.stem: Which flag combination expresses that restriction, and which statement about it is accurate?

options.text: `--disallowedTools "Bash"`. A bare tool name in this list removes the matching tool from Claude's context entirely rather than merely prompting on it.
`--allowedTools "Read" "Grep"`. Listing only the read-only tools means everything else falls through to the normal prompt, and since the runner has no terminal to prompt on, the calls are denied.
`--permission-mode dontAsk` together with `--allowedTools "Read" "Grep"`. In that mode anything not pre-approved is denied, which removes the job's ability to run anything outside the read-only set.

`--tools "Read,Grep,Glob"`. This restricts which built-in tools Claude can use — `default` for the default set, a comma-separated list for a narrower one, and `""` to disable all. The flag does not affect MCP tools, so a separate `--disallowedTools "mcp__*"` is needed to deny those too.

questions.explanation: There are three distinct tools and permissions switches and conflating them is the usual cause of an over- or under-restricted CI job. `--tools` restricts which built-in tools are available to Claude at all — `default` for the default set, a comma-separated list to narrow it, `""` to disable everything — which is what removes Bash from the pool rather than prompting on it. `--allowedTools` is different: it lists tools that execute without prompting, and it is a pre-approval mechanism, not a restriction. `--disallowedTools` is the deny list, and its behaviour depends on shape: a bare tool name such as `Edit` removes that tool from Claude's context, as does `"*"` for every tool and `"mcp__*"` for every MCP tool, whereas a scoped rule like `Bash(rm *)` leaves the tool available and denies only matching calls. Crucially `--tools` does not touch MCP tools, so denying those needs the `--disallowedTools "mcp__*"` form. In `dontAsk` mode anything not pre-approved is denied, which is a different guarantee: it withholds approval, it does not remove the tool from the model's context.

whyWrong.A: It reaches a similar destination by a route that also breaks the ability to read and edit files: removing Bash is right, but the reviewer asked for no command execution while keeping file tools, and this option as written does not say what happens to MCP tools.
whyWrong.B: Listing read-only tools in `--allowedTools` grants those and leaves everything else to a prompt. On a runner with no way to answer, that behaves like denial by accident rather than by design, and the tools are still advertised to the model.
whyWrong.C: `dontAsk` withholds approval for unlisted calls, which is a weaker and different property than removing the tool. It also says nothing about MCP tools, and a job that can still see Bash in its context can still try to call it.

questions.mindset: Three different switches: `--tools` changes the pool, `--allowedTools` pre-approves, `--disallowedTools` denies — only the first removes a tool from the model's context.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs runs an internal benchmark that shells out to `claude` on a shared evaluation host used by four teams. The host's user and project settings belong to whoever is logged in, and one team has already had a stray hook fire during someone else's benchmark run.
questions.stem: Which flag is designed for this situation, and what exactly does it enforce?

options.text: `--bare`. It skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, and it never reads OAuth credentials, so `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` must be set or an `apiKeyHelper` supplied. That is close to what is needed, but bare mode still honours the host's user and project settings, which is the part that cannot be left open on a shared machine.

`--restricted`. Claude Code removes the built-in tools that run commands or code, and WebFetch, unless you name them individually in `--tools` rather than through the `default` preset; it confines the built-in file tools to the working directories; it loads only managed settings and `--settings`; and it refuses `bypassPermissions` as well as cloud session creation. That is the isolation an evaluation harness on someone else's machine needs.

`--safe-mode`. It disables every customization — CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers, custom commands and agents, output styles, workflows, themes, keybindings, status line, file-suggestion commands, LSP servers and auto memory — while authentication, model selection, built-in tools and permissions work normally. Since it explicitly still loads the host's settings, it does not solve the shared-host problem.
No single flag does this. `--setting-sources project` restricts which settings files load, so pairing it with `--bare` and a `--tools` list is the only way to reach the isolation the benchmark needs.

questions.explanation: `--restricted` exists for exactly this case and is worth knowing separately from `--bare` and `--safe-mode`, which solve different problems. It is documented for the situation where an evaluation harness drives `claude` on a shared machine and Claude Code must not run commands or read that machine's user and project settings. Concretely: it removes the built-in tools that run commands or code, and WebFetch, unless you name them individually in `--tools` — naming them through the `default` preset does not bring them back; it confines the built-in file tools to the working directories; it loads only managed settings and `--settings`; it refuses `bypassPermissions`; and it refuses to create cloud sessions. Note what it does not do: it is not about starting faster (that is bare mode) and not about isolating one customization (that is safe mode).

whyWrong.A: Bare mode's credential behaviour is described correctly, but it addresses startup and reproducibility, not trust. It still reads the host's user and project settings, so a stray hook on a shared machine remains a possibility.
whyWrong.C: Safe mode's list is accurate and its closing clause is the disqualifier: managed settings policy still applies and the machine's own settings are not the thing it isolates. It is a troubleshooting flag for a broken customization.
whyWrong.D: It overstates the need for combination and misses the flag built for the case. `--setting-sources` restricts which settings files load, which is genuinely useful, but it does not remove command-running tools, confine file tools to the working directories, or refuse bypass permissions.

questions.mindset: Three flags, three jobs: `--bare` for fast reproducible scripts, `--safe-mode` to bisect one broken customization, `--restricted` to untrust the host.

questions.scenario: Meridian's sessions have started silently falling back to a different model. The team suspects a customization: a skill, a hook, or a CLAUDE.md rule that changes. They cannot remove the repository's configuration for a diagnosis.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about isolating the cause are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: `--safe-mode` starts with all customizations disabled to troubleshoot a broken configuration: CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers, custom commands and agents, output styles, workflows, custom themes, keybindings, status line and file-suggestion commands, LSP servers and auto memory do not load. Authentication, model selection, built-in tools and permissions work normally — which is why it, not bare mode, isolates a customization.

Managed settings policy still applies under `--safe-mode`, including policy-configured hooks, status line and file-suggestion commands, and managed plugins, managed skills, managed CLAUDE.md and policy-configured MCP servers do not load. That is deliberate: an administrator's controls are not the customization being debugged.
`--safe-mode` and `--bare` are interchangeable for this purpose. Both disable every customization, and the only difference is that bare mode additionally skips credential discovery.
Neither flag is appropriate: automatic model fallback is resolved by the API, so a local customization cannot trigger it and the diagnosis has to be done from the request logs.

questions.explanation: `--safe-mode` is the documented bisect for this exact question, and the docs name automatic model fallback as one of the things it is useful for. It disables the customization layer wholesale — CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers, custom commands and agents, output styles, workflows, custom themes, keybindings, status line and file-suggestion commands, LSP servers and auto memory — while leaving authentication, model selection, built-in tools and permissions working normally, which is the difference from bare mode. Managed settings policy still applies, including policy-configured hooks, status line and file-suggestion commands, while managed plugins, managed skills, managed CLAUDE.md and policy-configured MCP servers do not load. That asymmetry is the point: you are isolating the repository's and the user's customizations, not an administrator's controls. If the fallback disappears under safe mode, the cause is a customization and you can bisect further with `/reload-skills` and by disabling sources one at a time.

whyWrong.C: They are not interchangeable and the credential point is a red herring in this direction. `--safe-mode` keeps authentication, model selection, built-in tools and permissions working; `--bare` is aimed at starting faster and reproducing scripted runs, and it skips credential discovery as part of that, not as a debugging convenience.
whyWrong.D: A local customization absolutely can influence model selection — a skill or agent that sets `model`, a CLAUDE.md instruction to use a different model — so the hypothesis that only the request logs can answer it is wrong. Safe mode is the documented first move.

questions.mindset: To find which customization is causing behaviour, disable the whole customization layer with `--safe-mode` and bisect from there — managed policy deliberately stays on.

questions.scenario: Meridian's release notes are produced by a long scripted conversation. The script loops `claude -p --continue` with a different `--append-system-prompt` each pass, adding one house rule per iteration. After three passes the team realises none of the newly added rules are taking effect.
questions.stem: What is the documented reason, and what is the correct fix?

options.text: By default Claude Code builds the system prompt once, on a conversation's first request, with the text from any system prompt flags applied, and records it in the session. Every later request uses that recorded prompt — including after you come back to the conversation with `--resume` or `--continue` — until the conversation is compacted. Passing different system prompt flag text on a later launch takes effect once the conversation is compacted or you start a new conversation; pass `--system-prompt-snapshot off` to rebuild it on every request instead, which is the documented pattern for iterating on `--append-system-prompt` across `--continue` runs.

`--continue` discards system prompt flags entirely on resumption, so the flags only ever apply to a conversation's first request. Passing `--system-prompt-snapshot on` makes them apply from the second request onward.

Only `--system-prompt` and `--system-prompt-file` are subject to the recording. `--append-system-prompt` and `--append-system-prompt-file` are applied afresh on every request, because appending is additive and cannot invalidate anything already sent.
The problem is precedence rather than recording: the recorded prompt outranks `--append-system-prompt`, so the flag is applied and then discarded. `--system-prompt-snapshot off` does nothing here.

questions.explanation: This is a genuinely counter-intuitive behaviour and it is documented in detail under the system prompt flags. By default Claude Code builds the system prompt once, on a conversation's first request, with the text from any system prompt flags applied, and records it in the session. Until the conversation is compacted, every later request uses that recorded prompt — including after returning to the conversation with `--resume` or `--continue`. If you pass different system prompt flag text on that later launch, or none, it takes effect only once the conversation is compacted or you start a new conversation. For the exact use case in the scenario — iterating on `--append-system-prompt` wording across `--continue` runs — the documented answer is `--system-prompt-snapshot off`, which rebuilds the prompt on every request instead of reusing the recording. Two version caveats sit alongside it: in bare mode recording stays off unless you pass `--system-prompt-snapshot on`, and before v2.1.265, passing any of the system prompt flags also turned recording off unless you passed `on`.

whyWrong.B: It has the mechanism roughly right but inverts the remedy. `--continue` does not discard the flags — the recorded prompt is what the later launch is compared against — and `on` is the default, so asking for it changes nothing; `off` is what forces a rebuild.
whyWrong.C: Recording covers all five system prompt flags, not just the two that replace the prompt. Append flags are recorded too, which is exactly why the team's added rules stopped landing after the first pass.
whyWrong.D: This misfiles the cause as a precedence conflict. There is no contest between the recording and the flag at request time; the flag is read at the conversation's first request, and later edits wait for compaction unless recording is switched off.

questions.mindset: The system prompt is recorded on a conversation's first request and reused; if you are changing it mid-conversation, turn the recording off.

questions.scenario: Meridian's classification service sends a custom system prompt that is 4,000 tokens of invariant house rules followed by a per-record block that changes every request. Finance reports that the input line item dwarfs the output line item and that a cache read is never observed.
questions.stem: What is the documented way to keep the invariant part cached, and why does the current shape not achieve it?

options.text: Split the prompt at the API level by setting a cache breakpoint parameter on the request. Claude Code has no role in prefix identity, so the fix has to be made in the integration code.

Add a line containing only `__SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY__` between the invariant instructions and the per-record context. Claude Code splits the prompt at the first such line and removes the line itself, so the part above it stays cached while the part below it changes.
Convert the prompt to CLAUDE.md. Claude Code keeps CLAUDE.md stable across sessions, so the invariant rules become a cacheable prefix for free and the per-record context moves into the user message.
Nothing in Claude Code can help, because changing the system prompt with `--system-prompt` invalidates the cache on every request. The only lever is shortening the invariant text.

questions.explanation: There is a documented mechanism for exactly this shape, and it is a single marker line. When replacement system prompt text combines instructions that are the same on every run with context that changes per run, you add a line containing only `__SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY__` between the instructions and the context; Claude Code splits the prompt at the first such line and removes the line, so the text above stays cached and the text below changes. This is the CLI-side counterpart of the general caching rule: a cached prefix is only useful if the varying content sits after the breakpoint, because anything that changes earlier in the prefix breaks prefix identity and turns every read into a write. Note the reach: this works when you are supplying prompt text through the system prompt flags, which is why it is the right fix for a custom-prompt script rather than for a default Claude Code session.

whyWrong.A: It hands the problem to a layer that cannot solve it. Cache breakpoints are a property of how the request is assembled, and if your integration never asks for one, no parameter will rescue a prefix that changes on every call.
whyWrong.C: It confuses session stability with request stability. CLAUDE.md is stable across sessions but Claude Code still builds it into each request's prompt, and the per-record block appended after it still changes the prefix unless a boundary separates them.
whyWrong.D: Changing the prompt does not invalidate the cache by itself — invalidation comes from changing content that precedes the breakpoint. Using the documented boundary is precisely how you keep the invariant text cacheable while the varying text changes.

questions.mindset: If per-run context follows invariant text in the same prompt, separate them at the documented boundary so the invariant prefix stays cacheable.

questions.scenario: Meridian's committed `.claude/settings.json` defines a two-entry fallback chain, `sonnet,haiku`. An engineer's user settings define a different two-entry chain, `haiku`, and their local file defines a third. The team assumed the three chains would combine into one list. They do not.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about `fallbackModel` are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: `fallbackModel` is an ordered chain where position carries meaning, so Claude Code takes the whole value from the highest-precedence file that defines it. It is one of the list-shaped keys that deliberately does not merge, because a merged chain would have no defined order of preference.

The key follows the general list-merging rule that `permissions.allow` follows, so the engineer's session would fall back through `sonnet`, `haiku`, then the user and local entries — a longer, safer chain than any single file declares.

`fallbackModel` never applies from a committed project file at all. It is documented as `User or managed` scope, so a repository cannot ship a fallback chain and the team's committed entry has no effect on anyone but the person who wrote it.

The chain applies whenever the primary model is overloaded or not available, including for a retired model, and `--fallback-model` overrides the setting for a session while accepting a comma-separated list tried in order.

questions.explanation: `fallbackModel` is one of four keys that hold model lists or per-model entries and follow their own rules instead of merging. It is an ordered chain where position carries meaning, so Claude Code takes the whole value from the highest-precedence file that defines it — merging would produce a chain with no defined preference order, which defeats the point. Its behaviour is to enable automatic fallback to the specified model or models when the primary model is overloaded or not available, for example a retired model, and `--fallback-model` accepts a comma-separated list tried in order and overrides the setting for that session while the setting persists across sessions otherwise. The point for this team is the failure mode: a chain that silently changes shape depending on which file a given session happens to load is worse than no chain, so it belongs in one place at one scope.

whyWrong.B: It applies the general list-merging rule to the one case the docs carve out. Position in a fallback chain is the preference order, so Claude Code takes the whole highest-precedence value rather than combining files.
whyWrong.C: It invents a scope restriction. The committed project file does set `fallbackModel` for the session; the distinguishing feature of this key is the no-merge rule, not an inability to be delivered by a repository.

questions.mindset: Ordered keys do not merge: a fallback chain is taken whole from the highest-precedence file, so it has to live in exactly one place.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs has a legacy set of markdown command files in `.claude/commands/`, organised into subdirectories: `frontend/component.md`, `backend/migration.md` and `ops/rollback.md`. An engineer asks what to type to run the component one.
questions.stem: How does Claude Code derive the command name for a file in a subdirectory of `.claude/commands/`?

options.text: The subdirectory path relative to `commands/` with each `/` replaced by `:`, then the file name without its extension — so `frontend/component.md` is `/frontend:component`.
The file name alone, so `component.md` is `/component`, and the subdirectory is purely organisational with no effect on invocation.
The path relative to the working directory with slashes intact, so the command is `/frontend/component`.
The subdirectory is dropped unless the file also sets a `name` field, in which case the `name` supplies the command and the subdirectory is ignored entirely.

questions.explanation: The command name for a command file is derived from where the file lives, and subdirectories are part of that derivation. For a file in a subdirectory of `.claude/commands/`, it is the subdirectory path relative to `commands/` with each `/` replaced by `:`, then the file name without extension: `.claude/commands/frontend/component.md` gives `/frontend:component`. The same colon convention appears for nested skill directories, where `apps/web/.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` is `/apps/web:deploy`. Command files are the older format and still work, supporting the same frontmatter as a skill except `name` and `paths`; a skill wins a name clash with a command file, which is the other reason the docs recommend skills for new work since they also support supporting files.

whyWrong.B: It ignores the subdirectory, which is exactly the part of the name the subdirectory contributes. Two files named `component.md` in different subdirectories would collide under this rule.
whyWrong.C: It gets the source of the name right but the separator wrong. The convention replaces slashes with colons rather than keeping them, matching the nested-skill form `/apps/web:deploy`.
whyWrong.D: Command files do not support the `name` field at all — that is one of the two frontmatter fields a command file explicitly does not accept, alongside `paths`.

questions.mindset: Nested names use colons: a path relative to the base directory with `/` replaced by `:`, so structure in the filesystem becomes structure in the command.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs ships a project skill at `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md`. A platform engineer has been experimenting with `deploy` in `~/.claude/skills/deploy/`, and the security team has deployed the same name into the managed settings directory. Now `/deploy` behaves differently on three different machines and nobody can say which copy is running.
questions.stem: Which resolution rule explains the three behaviours, and what should the team do?

options.text: All three load and Claude picks between them at runtime based on which files it has read this session, so the behaviour varies with the working directory rather than with any ordering rule.
The project skill wins, because a file committed to the repository is closer to the work than anything installed on a machine, so all three machines would agree once they clone.
The enterprise copy loads for everyone, the personal copy loads for one person, and the project copy loads for anyone who clones — all three coexist and are distinguished by their location.

When the same name appears in two of the enterprise, personal and project locations, the order is enterprise over personal, and personal over project — so `/deploy` runs the personal copy on the engineer's machine and the enterprise copy elsewhere, and the project skill only runs where neither of the other two exists. Delete the experiment or rename it.

questions.explanation: Name resolution is by location, and the order is the opposite of what most people assume. When two of enterprise, personal and project share a name, enterprise wins over personal, and personal wins over project — so with `deploy` in both `~/.claude/skills/` and the project's `.claude/skills/`, `/deploy` runs the personal one. The documented table separates a few other cases: a skill and a file in `.claude/commands/` means the skill runs; a project-root skill and a nested skill with the same name means both load, with the root one under `/deploy` and the nested one addressable as `/apps/web:deploy`; and a plugin skill is namespaced as `/plugin-name:skill-name`, so it coexists with a local skill of the same name rather than competing. The same table shows that your skill replaces a bundled skill or a built-in command but not their aliases.

whyWrong.A: Resolution is decided statically by location, not per request by what has been read. A skill whose name collides with another command is simply never selected by that short name.
whyWrong.B: It assumes source control confers priority. Project scope sits below both enterprise and personal in the documented order, so the committed copy is the one that loses.
whyWrong.C: It describes coexistence, which is true for nested and plugin skills but not for the enterprise/personal/project trio. Those three compete for the same short name and only the highest-precedence one runs.

questions.mindset: A short name is won by location, in the order enterprise, personal, project — nesting and plugins add names rather than competing for one.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs writes a project skill at `.claude/skills/code-review/SKILL.md` and a second one at `.claude/skills/usage/SKILL.md`. Engineers report that typing `/code-review` and `/usage` run the project's skills, but `/review` and `/cost` still run the built-in behaviour — and one engineer insists this is a bug.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about replacing built-ins and bundled skills are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Nothing is happening. A skill named after a built-in command simply never loads, because those names are reserved the same way `synced` is.

This is documented behaviour. In a local terminal session your skill replaces a built-in command or a bundled skill, but not its aliases: a project `code-review` skill replaces `/code-review` while the bundled alias `/review` never runs your skill, and a project `usage` skill replaces `/usage` while the built-in alias `/cost` still runs the built-in command.
Only the first case is a replacement. `/usage` is a built-in command rather than a bundled skill, so a project skill cannot displace it and the command's own name is unavailable.
Aliases are only protected for skills synced from a claude.ai account. Locally authored skills take over every name and alias in the same family, which is why `/review` has not been checked yet.

questions.explanation: Replacement is real but deliberately narrow. In a local terminal session your skill replaces a built-in command or a bundled skill, and the docs call out the same two examples the team hit: a project `code-review` skill replaces `/code-review` while the bundled alias `/review` never runs your skill, and a project `usage` skill replaces `/usage` while the built-in alias `/cost` still runs the built-in command. So `/review` behaving normally is not a bug — the alias namespace stays with the built-in. The wider rule is the same one the docs apply to synced skills: when a synced skill from a claude.ai account collides with another command, `/<name>` runs the other command and the synced skill runs only as `/anthropic-skills:<name>`. Name comparison ignores case, spacing and invisible characters and treats look-alike Unicode forms as their plain equivalents, so a synced `Commit` and a local `commit` are one name — and the `claude.ai sync` label is how you tell the two apart in `/skills`, `/context` and the `/` menu.

whyWrong.A: It invents a reservation rule. Only specific names are reserved — `synced` for skills downloaded from claude.ai and the `anthropic-skills` namespace — and a skill named after a built-in loads and replaces it in a terminal session.
whyWrong.C: It splits built-in commands from bundled skills for no documented reason. The replacement rule covers both, and the table names `/usage` against the built-in alias `/cost` explicitly.

questions.mindset: Your skill takes the built-in's name but not its aliases, and a synced skill that loses its short name moves to the reserved `anthropic-skills:` namespace.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs has two skills that silently fail to load. One sits at `~/.claude/skills/synced/SKILL.md`, written by hand. The other is a project skill whose frontmatter declares `name: anthropic-skills:pdf`. Neither produces an error in the session.
questions.stem: What is happening in each case, and what should Vireo Labs do?

options.text: `synced` is reserved in any capitalization for the directory Claude Code uses for skills downloaded from claude.ai, and a skill you author at that name in the enterprise, personal or project location is skipped. `anthropic-skills` is reserved as a namespace so a synced skill's full name never runs something else — a skill folder, a frontmatter `name`, a file or subfolder in `.claude/commands/`, or a saved workflow with that name does not load, and a startup notice names the first item to rename. Rename both.

`synced` is reserved but case-sensitively, so `Synced` would have been fine. `anthropic-skills` is only reserved for plugins: a plugin named `anthropic-skills` loads, and when one of its skills and a synced skill share a name, `/anthropic-skills:<name>` runs the synced skill.
Both are ordinary name collisions that a later skill silently overwrites. Rename either one and the problem resolves itself.
The `anthropic-skills` namespace is reserved only in sessions signed in to a claude.ai account. On an API-key-authenticated session the reservation does not apply and both skills load normally.

questions.explanation: Two names are reserved, for two different reasons, and both fail silently in the sense that no error stops the session. `~/.claude/skills/synced/` is where Claude Code puts skills downloaded from a claude.ai account, so a skill folder named `synced` in any capitalization in the enterprise, personal or project location is skipped. `anthropic-skills` is reserved as a namespace so a synced skill's full name can never run something else; the reserved forms are a skill folder, a frontmatter `name`, a file or subfolder in `.claude/commands/`, and a saved workflow — and none of them load. The reservation holds in every session whether or not anyone is signed in to a claude.ai account. Two related details are worth knowing: a plugin named `anthropic-skills` does load, in which case `/anthropic-skills:<name>` runs the synced skill, and an MCP server by that name connects and works but its prompts do not appear as commands.

whyWrong.B: It inverts both rules. The `synced` reservation is case-insensitive, so `Synced` fails too, and the `anthropic-skills` reservation is wider than plugins — it also covers local skill folders, command files and workflows. The plugin behaviour it describes is the documented exception, not the general case.
whyWrong.C: The names are exactly the cause here, and a missing `description` has a different symptom — the skill loads and appears in the listing with a description taken from its first non-empty markdown line. These two never load at all.
whyWrong.D: The reservation is unconditional. The docs state that `anthropic-skills` is reserved in every session, whether or not you sign in to a claude.ai account, precisely so the namespace is stable.

questions.mindset: Two reserved names — `synced` in any capitalization, and the `anthropic-skills` namespace — and an item using either does not load at all.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs' `triage-ledger` skill has a correct YAML frontmatter block, but Claude never invokes it automatically — only the explicit `/triage-ledger` works. An engineer inspects the file and sees a blank line before the opening `---`.
questions.stem: What is Claude Code doing with that file, and what is the fix?

options.text: The YAML is parsed but the leading blank line puts it in a code block, so every field is read as a string and the booleans silently become `"true"`. Replace `true` with `yes` and it will work.

Frontmatter is read only when the opening `---` is the file's first line; otherwise Claude Code treats the whole file, `---` markers included, as skill content. It also reads frontmatter only when the YAML between the markers parses — if it does not, the skill still loads with no fields set. The fix is to make `---` line one; a robust team lints for this because the failure is silent.
Nothing is wrong with the file. Claude Code tolerates leading whitespace before the frontmatter and only requires the closing `---` to be exact, so the real problem is elsewhere.

The skill is loading with its fields intact but Claude declines to auto-invoke it because the description is under the length cap. Cap compliance is checked against the invocation decision, so a shorter description is treated as insufficient.

questions.explanation: The parsing rule is exact and positional, which is what makes this such a common silent failure. Claude Code reads the frontmatter only when the opening `---` is the file's first line; otherwise it treats the whole file, `---` markers included, as skill content. There is a second tolerance worth knowing in the same place: if the YAML between the markers does not parse, the skill still loads with no fields set. Both failure modes are silent, and both have the same visible symptom here — `description` is what Claude reads when deciding whether to apply a skill, so a skill that never gets its fields parsed simply never auto-invokes. The fix is to make `---` line one of the file. Related tolerance that is genuine: boolean fields accept `yes`, `no`, `on`, `off`, `1` and `0` in any letter case in addition to `true` and `false`, so that is not what is going on here.

whyWrong.A: It invents a code-fence effect and a string-coercion problem. The rule is positional — the opening `---` must be the first line — and the whole file becomes content rather than the fields being mistyped.
whyWrong.C: It claims a tolerance the docs do not promise. There is no allowance for leading whitespace before the opening marker; that is exactly the condition described.
whyWrong.D: It confuses the truncation cap with the invocation decision. The 1,536-character cap truncates `description` plus `when_to_use` in the skill listing to control context usage; it does not gate whether Claude may consider a skill at all.

questions.mindset: Frontmatter is positional and fail-silent: `---` must be line one, and unparseable YAML loads the skill with no fields.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs' `deep-audit` skill sets `model: opus` in its frontmatter because the audit needs more reasoning than the session default. Engineers are surprised that the rest of the conversation after `/deep-audit` runs on whatever the session model was, and that a model their organization disallows is quietly not used.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about a skill's `model` field are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: The override applies for the rest of the current turn and is not saved to settings; the session model resumes when you send your next prompt. The field accepts the same values as `/model`, or `inherit` to keep the active model.

A value excluded by your organization's `availableModels` allowlist is not used and the session keeps its current model. The same rule applies in auto mode, and in plan mode while the classifier reviews commands, for a model auto mode does not support.
The field pins the model for the rest of the session, which is why the engineers observed the change persisting after the skill ran. It can only be undone by restarting Claude Code.

The field is ignored entirely for skills that use `context: fork`, since the forked subagent always runs on the parent session's model. That is the documented behaviour and the reason the audit ran on the session model.

questions.explanation: A skill's `model` field is deliberately turn-scoped, which is what the engineers observed. The override applies for the rest of the current turn and isn't saved to settings, and the session model resumes when you send your next prompt. It accepts the same values as `/model`, or `inherit` to keep the active model. The allowlist interaction is the second half and it is the safety property: a value excluded by your organization's `availableModels` allowlist isn't used, and the session keeps its current model; the same exclusion applies in auto mode and in plan mode while the classifier reviews commands, for a model auto mode does not support. With `context: fork` the value instead sets the forked subagent's model, and an excluded value follows the same rules as a subagent model override. There is also an `effort` field for the skill's turn, which overrides the session effort level and resolves from the effort order when omitted.

whyWrong.C: It inverts the lifecycle. The override is turn-scoped by design precisely so a skill cannot quietly re-model the rest of somebody's session.
whyWrong.D: It asserts the opposite of the documented behaviour. With `context: fork` the `model` value sets the forked subagent's model, which is an additional effect rather than an exclusion.

questions.mindset: A skill's `model` and `effort` fields shape the turn that invokes them, and an allowlisted-out model is skipped rather than substituted.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs has accumulated a set of conventions that Claude should apply whenever it touches payment code — naming rules, the state-machine shape, the anti-patterns the team rejects. Nobody wants these to appear as slash commands, and typing them by hand would be noise in the `/` menu.
questions.stem: Which frontmatter setting expresses that, and how does it differ from the alternative?

options.text: `disable-model-invocation: true`. Claude will not load the skill on its own, so it stops triggering automatically — the opposite of what this conventions set needs.

`user-invocable: false`. Claude Code hides the skill from the `/` menu and does not run it when you type `/name`, which is exactly right for background knowledge users should not invoke directly. It defaults to `true`. The counterpart, `disable-model-invocation: true`, goes the other way: it stops Claude from loading the skill automatically and is what you set on a workflow you want to trigger manually.
`skillOverrides` with the entry set to `"name-only"` in settings. That keeps the description in the listing but hides the body from `/`, which is what stops it appearing in the menu.
`disableBundledSkills: true`. With bundled skills off, only local skills appear, so a project conventions file will not clutter the menu.

questions.explanation: The two invocation fields point in opposite directions and picking the wrong one silently disables the behaviour you wanted. `user-invocable: false` is the one for background knowledge: Claude Code hides the skill from the `/` menu and does not run it when you type `/name`, and it defaults to `true`. `disable-model-invocation: true` does the reverse — it stops Claude from automatically loading the skill, which is what you set on a task-style workflow you want to trigger manually, and it also prevents the skill being preloaded into subagents and from running when a scheduled task fires with it as the prompt. For a conventions set that Claude should apply on its own when relevant, the correct configuration is the default on both counts: leave `user-invocable` alone if the team is happy to see it in the menu, and leave `disable-model-invocation` at `false` so it can trigger. `skillOverrides` is for visibility — `"off"` to hide, `"user-invocable-only"` to stop Claude invoking without editing the file.

whyWrong.A: It names the right field for the wrong goal. `disable-model-invocation: true` would prevent Claude from applying the conventions automatically, which is the opposite of what a background-knowledge skill is for.
whyWrong.C: `"name-only"` controls the skill listing budget, not menu visibility. It keeps a name in the listing while trimming descriptions, which is a context-cost lever rather than a way to hide an entry from the `/` menu.
whyWrong.D: `disableBundledSkills` turns off Claude Code's own bundled skills such as `/doctor`, `/code-review` and `/verify`. It has no effect on whether a project skill appears in the menu.

questions.mindset: Two opposite switches: `user-invocable: false` hides a skill from humans, `disable-model-invocation: true` hides it from Claude. Background knowledge wants both defaults.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs wants one skill to work in the terminal, in Claude Desktop, and in scheduled runs — so they enable it on the team's claude.ai account and package it with `package_skill.py`. The upload fails with `Unexpected key(s) in SKILL.md frontmatter: argument-hint`.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about frontmatter portability are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Claude Code accepts every frontmatter field, but outside Claude Code you may use only the fields in the Agent Skills spec: `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata` and `allowed-tools`. That covers claude.ai skill uploads, the Skills API, and `package_skill.py` from `anthropics/skills`.

The failure is a hard error, not a silent drop: including a field the spec does not allow makes packaging or upload fail with an unexpected-key message rather than ignoring the field. Restricting frontmatter to the six spec fields avoids it, and since Claude Code accepts all six, a spec-compliant skill loads in Claude Code unchanged.
The field is stripped during packaging and the upload proceeds. This is a warning you can ignore, because `argument-hint` only affects the terminal's autocomplete.

Enabling the skill on a claude.ai account is what makes the packaging failure occur. Uploading is only restricted for skills that stay local, so the fix is to package it before enabling it on the account.

questions.explanation: The portability boundary is explicit and it is worth knowing before you design a skill for more than one surface. Claude Code accepts every field in its frontmatter reference. Outside Claude Code you may use only the Agent Skills spec fields: `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata` and `allowed-tools`. That applies to claude.ai skill uploads, the Skills API, and packaging with `package_skill.py` from `anthropics/skills`. And it is a hard error rather than a silent drop — packaging or upload fails with `Unexpected key(s) in SKILL.md frontmatter: ... Allowed properties are: allowed-tools, compatibility, description, license, metadata, name`. Two consequences follow for a team standardising one skill across surfaces: restricting frontmatter to those six fields avoids the failure and still loads in Claude Code unchanged, since Claude Code accepts all six; and Claude Code-only body features such as dynamic context injection with a backtick command line do not function in claude.ai chat or through the API at all. Separately, a skill that exists only in `~/.claude/skills/` will not be found by a scheduled claude.ai run, because each run starts as a fresh cloud session that does not read your machine's personal skills directory.

whyWrong.C: It downgrades a hard error to a warning. The docs are explicit that packaging or upload fails with an unexpected-key error instead of ignoring the field, which is the entire point of validating the spec subset.
whyWrong.D: It has the causality backwards. The restriction is a property of the packaging and upload paths themselves, not of whether the skill is also enabled on a claude.ai account; ordering the steps differently would not help.

questions.mindset: Claude Code accepts every frontmatter field; portability paths accept six — and an extra field is a hard packaging error, not a silent drop.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs' `/promote` skill takes an environment and a service name. The current body reads `Promote $0 to $1`, which breaks whenever someone passes the arguments in the other order or supplies only one.
questions.stem: Which frontmatter and body combination gives named arguments, and what are the documented substitution rules?

options.text: `arguments: [environment, service]` plus a body line reading `Promote $service in $environment`. Names map to argument positions in order, and `$name` is a named placeholder declared in the `arguments` field, which accepts a space-separated string or a YAML list. The related forms are `$ARGUMENTS` for everything typed, `$ARGUMENTS[N]` for one by 0-based index, and `$N` as shorthand for `$ARGUMENTS[N]`.
`args: environment service` plus `$environment` and `$service` in the body. `args` is the documented field name for declaring positional arguments in skill frontmatter.
`arguments: environment, service` is correct, but only `$ARGUMENTS[environment]` resolves it by name. The bare `$name` form is reserved for command files and does not work in a skill.
No frontmatter can name arguments. Positional substitution is the only mechanism, so the skill must parse `$ARGUMENTS` itself and infer the order from the surrounding instructions.

questions.explanation: Named positional arguments are a documented frontmatter field, and the distinction between them and `argument-hint` is the usual source of confusion. `arguments` declares named positional arguments for substitution in the skill content and accepts a space-separated string or a YAML list; names map to argument positions in order, so `arguments: [issue, branch]` makes `$issue` the first argument and `$branch` the second. The full substitution surface is worth holding together: `$ARGUMENTS` is everything passed, and when no placeholder receives an argument Claude Code appends them as `ARGUMENTS: <value>`; `$ARGUMENTS[N]` accesses one by 0-based index; `$N` is shorthand for `$ARGUMENTS[N]`; `$name` is a declared named argument; and there are session and path placeholders — `${CLAUDE_SESSION_ID}`, `${CLAUDE_EFFORT}`, `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`, `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}`, plus `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` and `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` in plugin skills. `argument-hint` is separate: it is the autocomplete hint shown in the prompt, not a declaration.

whyWrong.B: It invents a field name. The field is `arguments`, and note that frontmatter field names use lowercase words separated by hyphens except `when_to_use` — there is no `args` key to read.
whyWrong.C: It keeps the field and mangles the substitution. `$name` is precisely the documented form for a declared named argument, and the indexed form is `$ARGUMENTS[N]` where N is a 0-based index, not a name.
whyWrong.D: It claims a limit that does not exist. The `arguments` field exists for exactly this, and declaring names is what makes a skill robust to callers varying their argument order.

questions.mindset: `arguments` declares named positional substitution; `argument-hint` only hints at autocomplete. Use `$name` for names, `$N` for positions.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs has a `terraform-review` skill. Its description mentions Terraform, and Claude invokes it during unrelated work because the word appears in a passing comment. The team wants it to load automatically only while working with `.tf` files and `.tfvars`.
questions.stem: What is the correct mechanism, and what are its semantics?

options.text: Put `disable-model-invocation: true` in the frontmatter. That is the documented way to keep Claude from choosing a skill on its own, and file matching happens inside the skill body.

Move the skill's description into the repository CLAUDE.md so it only loads when Claude reads that file. Skill activation is deliberately independent of instruction files, which is why this would not change the behaviour.

Set `paths` in the frontmatter with the globs, as a comma-separated string or a YAML list. When set, Claude loads the skill automatically only when working with files matching those patterns, using the same format as path-specific rules.
Rename the directory so the name is more specific, for example `terraform-hcl-files-review`. Skill selection is driven by the directory name rather than the description, so renaming is the fix.

questions.explanation: Skills have their own path-scoped activation, and it uses the same glob format as path-specific rules so one mental model covers both. Setting `paths` in the frontmatter — a comma-separated string or a YAML list of glob patterns — means Claude loads the skill automatically only when working with files matching those patterns. That is the mechanism for narrowing automatic activation without giving up automatic invocation. It is worth placing next to the other conditional-loading surfaces, because teams conflate them: a rule with no `paths` loads at launch and a path-scoped rule waits for a matching file to be read or edited, while a skill's `paths` narrows the point at which the skill is eligible at all. And because selection is driven by the description in the skill listing, narrowing a description is still the first thing to try when a skill over-triggers generally — a `paths` field fixes over-triggering across file types, not a description that is too broad about intent.

whyWrong.A: It removes the behaviour the team wants to keep. `disable-model-invocation: true` stops Claude from ever loading the skill automatically, so `paths` would have no automatic trigger left to constrain.
whyWrong.B: It changes where text lives, not how skill activation works. A description in CLAUDE.md is an instruction Claude reads; it is not the listing entry the selection decision is made against.
whyWrong.D: It misattributes selection to the directory name. The directory name supplies the command when no `name` field is set; what Claude weighs when deciding whether to load a skill is its description and `when_to_use`.

questions.mindset: `paths` scopes when a skill is eligible; the description decides whether it is chosen. Fix over-triggering by file type with `paths`, not by renaming.

questions.scenario: Vireo Labs' `render-report` skill folder also carries a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, so it loads as a plugin named `render-report@skills-dir` and bundles hooks, an MCP server and an agent alongside the skill. The team edits `SKILL.md` mid-session and sees the change immediately, but edits to the bundled `hooks/` never take effect.
questions.stem: What is the documented reason, and what should Vireo Labs do?

options.text: Hooks declared inside a plugin are only read at session start by design, because plugin hooks must be validated against the plugin manifest. Restarting after every hook edit is expected.

Live change detection covers skill text, not plugin components. Claude Code watches skill directories and picks up `SKILL.md` changes within the current session, but for a skill folder that is also a plugin, changes to `hooks/`, `.mcp.json`, `agents/` and `output-styles/` need `/reload-plugins`. A related trap: if you created a top-level skills directory that did not exist when the session started, run `/reload-skills` to pick it up, and again after each later change there, because Claude Code is not watching that directory.

Neither mechanism applies. Once a skill folder is a plugin, all of its contents are governed by the plugin lifecycle, so `SKILL.md` edits also need a plugin reload and the observed immediate effect must have been a cached read.

The hook change did apply. Plugin hooks are registered when the plugin loads and are re-registered from disk on each invocation, so the problem is that the hook's own condition was wrong rather than the reload path.

questions.explanation: Two watchers with two scopes, and the boundary is documented. Claude Code watches skill directories for file changes and picks up `SKILL.md` additions, edits and removals within the current session without a restart — which is what the team observed. That live detection is limited to `SKILL.md` text: for a skill folder that is also a plugin, changes to `hooks/`, `.mcp.json`, `agents/` and `output-styles/` need `/reload-plugins` to take effect. The companion trap is the directory itself: if you create a top-level skills directory that did not exist when the session started, run `/reload-skills` to pick up what you put there, and again after each later change there, because Claude Code is not watching a directory it did not see at startup. Bare mode and safe mode both disable this watching, which is a further reason those two flags are poor choices for interactive authoring.

whyWrong.A: It attributes the behaviour to manifest validation, which is not the documented mechanism. Plugin components simply fall outside skill live-change detection and have their own explicit reload command.
whyWrong.C: It reverses the observed behaviour. `SKILL.md` edits taking effect immediately is exactly what skill live-change detection does; only the plugin components sit outside it.
whyWrong.D: It asserts the change applied and moves the blame to the hook condition. If the edit never reaches the plugin's hook registry in a running session, no condition inside the hook file can change that.

questions.mindset: Skill text hot-reloads; a skill folder that is also a plugin has components that need `/reload-plugins`, and a new skills directory needs `/reload-skills`.
